_about: Who can buy a home where, by nationality group (the data behind /can-i-buy)

meta.note: Who can buy a home where, by nationality group. General information compiled from the rules summarised in destinations.json and public government sources; not legal advice. Status: yes = same terms as locals or no permit needed; conditions = possible, with a permit, a trust, a company or a limit; restricted = not possible for most buyers who do not live there. Blocs: eu = EU citizens, eea = Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein (falls back to eu), ch = Switzerland (falls back to other), other = everyone else. A per-nationality key overrides the bloc.

american.label: American
notes: The US taxes its citizens on worldwide income, so rent from a home abroad goes on your US return, and foreign bank accounts above US$10,000 in total need an FBAR report.
Some banks abroad are slow to open accounts for US citizens because of FATCA reporting, so ask early.

british.label: British
notes: Since Brexit, British buyers count as non-EU buyers, so the non-EU rules and tax rates apply (for example on rental income).

canadian.label: Canadian
notes: Canadian residents whose foreign property costs more than CAD 100,000 in total must file form T1135 with the CRA.

australian.label: Australian
notes: Australian tax residents are taxed on worldwide income, so rent from a home abroad goes on your Australian return, usually with a credit for tax paid abroad.

dutch.label: Dutch
notes: Dutch residents declare a home abroad in box 3 (savings and investments) of their Dutch tax return.

norwegian.label: Norwegian
notes: Norway is not in the EU, but as part of the EEA, Norwegians buy and move on almost the same terms as EU citizens inside the EU.

spanish.label: Spanish
notes: Spanish residents with assets abroad above €50,000 in a category (such as property) must file form 720.

italian.label: Italian
notes: Italian residents declare property abroad in the RW section of their tax return and may owe IVIE, the tax on foreign property.

swiss.label: Swiss
notes: Switzerland is not in the EU or the EEA. The Swiss-EU free movement agreement lets Swiss citizens live in EU countries, but property rules for non-EU buyers can still apply.

eu.a: Yes. Since 2012 EU and EEA citizens can own both buildings and land in Bulgaria on the same terms as Bulgarians.

other.a: Yes, with a condition: {plural} can own apartments and buildings directly, but not the land under a house. The usual route for a house with a plot is a Bulgarian company, which can own land.

bulgaria.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in Bulgaria; longer stays need a residence permit.

all.a: Mostly not for now: a federal ban stops non-Canadians from buying homes in cities and larger towns until 1 January 2027. It does not cover rural areas and small towns, and there are exceptions, such as some work permit holders. Check the current status before you look: the government has said a replacement is being studied.

canada.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in Canada.

eu.a: Yes. EU citizens buy homes in Cyprus without restrictions.

other.a: Yes, with a permit: {plural} need permission from the Council of Ministers, applied for through the District Officer, and are normally limited to one home or a plot of up to 4,014 m². The permit is a formality for most buyers, but it takes time.

cyprus.residency_other: Non-EU buyers of a new home worth at least €300,000 plus VAT can apply for permanent residency under the Cyprus investment route; the conditions were tightened in 2023, so check the current rules.

eu.a: Only if you live there: {plural} who live and are registered in Denmark can buy a home they live in all year without permission, by signing a declaration. Without Danish residence you need permission from the Department of Civil Affairs (Civilstyrelsen), and holiday homes (sommerhuse) are only allowed for people with strong, long ties to Denmark.

other.a: Restricted. Without Danish residence (or 5 years of past residence) {plural} need permission from the Department of Civil Affairs (Civilstyrelsen), which is rarely given just to buy a home. Holiday homes (sommerhuse) are only allowed for people with strong, long ties to Denmark.

denmark.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in Denmark.

all.a: Yes. {plural} have the same rights as Dominican citizens to buy land and homes, with no restrictions.

dominican-republic.residency_other: Buying a home does not by itself give you residency in the Dominican Republic.

all.a: Yes. {plural} can buy property in France without restrictions and need no permit.

france.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in France; stays over 90 days need a long-stay visa.

all.a: Yes. There are no restrictions on {plural} buying property in Germany.

other.a: Yes. There are no restrictions on {plural} buying property in Germany, though banks usually ask non-EU buyers for a bigger down payment.

germany.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in Germany.

eu.a: Yes. EU citizens buy in Greece on the same terms as Greeks.

ch.a: Yes. EFTA citizens, including the Swiss, buy in Greece like EU citizens, including in the border areas.

other.a: Yes, with one condition: {plural} need a permit to buy in designated border areas (parts of northern Greece and eastern Aegean islands such as Rhodes and the Dodecanese). Elsewhere you buy like a Greek. The government has also announced a 15% transfer tax for non-EU buyers from 1 January 2027, not yet final.

greece.residency_other: Greece has a golden visa for non-EU buyers. Since 2024 the minimum is €800,000 in Attica, Thessaloniki, Mykonos, Santorini and larger islands, and €400,000 elsewhere, so a cheap home does not qualify.

eu.a: Yes. EU citizens buy in Italy on the same terms as Italians.

other.a: Yes. Italy lets non-EU citizens buy when their country lets Italians buy (reciprocity), and the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Switzerland all qualify. You need an Italian tax code (codice fiscale).

italy.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in Italy; stays over 90 days need a visa, such as the elective residence visa.

all.a: Yes. {plural} can buy freehold land and homes on the same terms as Japanese citizens, even on a tourist visa.

japan.residency_other: Buying a home gives no visa or residency in Japan.

all.a: Yes, with conditions. In the Restricted Zone (within 50 km of the coast or 100 km of the borders, which covers Tulum and Playa del Carmen) {plural} buy through a fideicomiso bank trust or a Mexican company. Inland you can own directly, with a permit from the Foreign Ministry.

mexico.residency_other: Buying a home gives no residency in Mexico; temporary residency is usually based on income or savings and applied for at a Mexican consulate.

all.a: Yes. There are no nationality or residence rules and no surcharge for foreign buyers in the Netherlands. Some cities restrict renting out cheaper homes after you buy (opkoopbescherming).

netherlands.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in the Netherlands.

all.a: Yes. Anyone with the funds can buy property in Norway, and a built plot of up to 2 decares normally needs no concession (konsesjon). Farms and larger plots need a concession.

norway.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in Norway.

eu.a: Yes. EU, EEA and Swiss citizens buy in Poland on the same terms as Poles.

ch.a: Yes. EU, EEA and Swiss citizens buy in Poland on the same terms as Poles.

other.a: Partly: {plural} can buy an apartment without a permit, but usually need a permit from the Ministry of the Interior (MSWiA) to buy a house or land.

poland.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in Poland.

all.a: Yes. {plural} buy in Portugal with the same rights as Portuguese citizens. You need a Portuguese tax number (NIF).

portugal.residency_other: Since October 2023, buying a home no longer qualifies for Portugal's golden visa. The D7 visa for people with passive income is the usual route to live there.

eu.a: Yes. EU citizens buy in Spain on the same terms as Spaniards. You need an NIE, your foreigner tax number.

other.a: Yes, for now. {plural} buy in Spain on the same terms as Spaniards and need an NIE, the foreigner tax number. The government has proposed a 100% tax on (or a ban for) non-EU buyers who do not live in Spain; it is not law as of November 2026, so check before you sign.

spain.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in Spain: the golden visa for property buyers closed on 3 April 2025. The non-lucrative visa is the usual route for people with passive income.

all.a: Yes. There are no citizenship or residence rules for buying a home in Sweden. You need a Swedish personal identity number or a coordination number (samordningsnummer) to register ownership.

sweden.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in Sweden.

eu.a: Only if you live there. Under the Lex Koller law, {plural} living in Switzerland buy like Swiss citizens. Living abroad, you need a cantonal permit and can usually only buy one holiday home in a tourist area, within national quotas.

other.a: Restricted. Under the Lex Koller law, {plural} living abroad need a cantonal permit and can usually only buy one holiday home in a tourist area, within national quotas. Living in Switzerland, holders of a C permit buy like Swiss citizens, and holders of a B permit can buy the home they live in.

switzerland.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in Switzerland.

all.a: Yes. There are no nationality restrictions on buying homes anywhere in the UK. In England and Northern Ireland, buyers who do not live in the UK pay a 2% stamp duty surcharge.

irish.a: Yes. There are no nationality restrictions on buying homes anywhere in the UK, and Irish citizens can also live and work there under the Common Travel Area. Buyers who do not live in the UK pay a 2% stamp duty surcharge in England and Northern Ireland.

united-kingdom.residency_other: Buying a home gives no right to live in the UK. Visitors can usually stay up to 6 months, and most now need an electronic travel authorisation (ETA) before they travel.

all.a: Yes. There is no federal ban on foreigners buying homes in the US. About 30 states have added some limits, mostly on farmland or on buyers from certain countries such as China, which do not affect {plural}.

united-states.residency_other: Buying a home gives no visa or right to live in the US; visits follow the normal visitor rules for your passport.
